title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Ink-Stained Sari: 'Ganga and Yamuna Have Met!'
summary: While Gandhi was writing letters with an ink fountain pen at Sevagram, an ashram sister accidentally tipped the bottle, spilling deep blue ink over her pristine white khadi sari. Seeing her near tears, Gandhi laughed gently: 'Do not cry, dear sister! The dark waters of Yamuna have simply flowed into your sacred white Ganga!'
keywords: Mahatma Gandhi and the Ink-Stained Sari: 'Ganga and Yamuna Have Met!'
full_text:
At Sevagram Ashram in Wardha, Mahatma Gandhi sat on his thin floor mat, writing urgent dispatches to national leaders with a wooden nib pen. An earthenware inkwell rested beside his low writing desk.

An young ashram sister arrived carrying a brass tray of peeled fruits. As she placed the tray down, her elbow accidentally caught the inkpot, sending black-blue fountain pen ink splashing directly across the front pleats of her pristine, hand-spun white khadi sari.

Horrified by what she had done, the young woman stood frozen, her eyes brimming with tears of shame and embarrassment before the Father of the Nation.

Gandhi looked up from his parchment. Instead of an angry scowl or a reprimand for wasting ink and ruining cloth, Gandhi broke into a merry, childlike chuckle.

"Why are your eyes weeping, my child?" Gandhi asked tenderly.

"Bapu... I have ruined my sari with ugly black stains, and wasted your precious ink," she sobbed.

Gandhi stood up, gently patted her shoulder, and said:
"Ruined? Who told you it is ruined? Look closely! Your white khadi sari represents the sparkling, pure white waters of Mother Ganga. And this deep blue ink represents the serene, mystic currents of Mother Yamuna. Today, right here in our Sevagram hut, the sacred Sangam has taken place! You are wearing a confluence of holy rivers. Go wash it with warm soap; you will find that even mistakes can look artistic when met with a smile!"

The young woman's tears vanished, replaced by a radiant smile. Ashram inmates who witnessed the moment realized that Gandhi's greatness lay not merely in leading millions in satyagraha, but in his infinite tenderness toward the feelings of ordinary souls.
